title: Hypothyroidism: Diagnose the Axis, Dose Levothyroxine Safely
bottomLine: Primary hypothyroidism is usually diagnosed and monitored with TSH, adding free T4 when indicated; central hypothyroidism requires free T4 because TSH can be misleading. Levothyroxine dosing depends on age, cardiac disease, pregnancy, body size, absorption and adherence—not one universal weight formula.
recognize: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia and menstrual changes are common but nonspecific.
Central disease is suggested by pituitary symptoms or low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH.
differentiate: Subclinical hypothyroidism has elevated TSH with normal free T4 and does not automatically require treatment in every patient.
Nonthyroidal illness and assay interference can distort results during acute illness.
assessment: Review pregnancy/planning, coronary disease, pituitary symptoms, medications/supplements, levothyroxine timing, iron/calcium, adherence and GI malabsorption risk.
workup: Use TSH first for most primary disease and free T4 when TSH is abnormal or central disease is possible; avoid routine free T3 testing for primary hypothyroidism.
management: Use levothyroxine and titrate with appropriate follow-up; start more cautiously in older adults/significant coronary disease and increase requirements promptly in pregnancy according to current thyroid guidance.
medicationSafety: Iron, calcium and selected medications impair absorption; over-replacement increases AF/bone risk and under-replacement can worsen symptoms/lipids/pregnancy outcomes.
Do not use TSH alone to titrate known central hypothyroidism.
counselling: Teach consistent administration and separation from interfering supplements; explain why dose changes are reassessed after steady state rather than daily symptoms.
followUp: Repeat thyroid testing at the clinically appropriate interval after dose change and more frequently in pregnancy or unstable disease.
examTrap: Increasing levothyroxine because free T4 is low-normal despite a normal TSH in uncomplicated primary hypothyroidism—or using TSH as the only guide in pituitary disease.
oneLinePearl: TSH guides primary hypothyroidism; free T4 rescues the cases where the pituitary cannot be trusted.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Endocrinology and Metabolism recommendations

title: Hyperthyroidism: Confirm Thyrotoxicosis, Then Find the Cause
bottomLine: A suppressed TSH with elevated thyroid hormone confirms primary thyrotoxicosis, but treatment depends on cause. Graves/toxic nodular disease produces excess synthesis; thyroiditis releases preformed hormone and does not improve from escalating antithyroid drugs. Thyroid storm is a clinical emergency, not an extreme lab value alone.
recognize: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, diarrhea, proximal weakness and AF are common; older adults may present with apathy or isolated arrhythmia.
Graves disease may cause diffuse goitre, ophthalmopathy and positive receptor antibodies.
differentiate: Thyroiditis, exogenous thyroid hormone and iodine/drug effects differ from Graves/toxic nodular hyperthyroidism.
Pregnancy changes physiologic ranges, imaging choices and antithyroid-drug selection.
assessment: Assess HR/rhythm, HF, eye/neck findings, pregnancy, amiodarone/iodine, biotin, medications, fever/CNS symptoms and precipitating infection.
workup: Use TSH/free thyroid hormone, receptor antibodies and selective uptake/imaging when needed to establish cause; do not order thyroid ultrasound solely for abnormal thyroid function without palpable structural abnormality.
management: Use cause-specific beta blockade when appropriate, antithyroid medication, radioiodine or surgery through current endocrine pathways; thyroid storm requires emergency multidrug treatment and precipitant control.
medicationSafety: Methimazole/PTU can cause agranulocytosis/hepatotoxicity; fever/sore throat requires urgent assessment. Pregnancy alters drug choice/timing.
counselling: Teach medication toxicity warning signs and smoking cessation for thyroid eye disease.
followUp: Trend thyroid function with treatment and plan definitive therapy/relapse monitoring according to cause.
examTrap: Escalating methimazole for thyroiditis because the T4 remains elevated without proving excess hormone synthesis.
oneLinePearl: Thyrotoxicosis is the state; the cause determines whether antithyroid drugs can work.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Endocrinology/Nuclear Medicine recommendations

title: Thyroid Nodule: TSH, Ultrasound Risk, Then FNA When Indicated
bottomLine: A thyroid nodule needs structural risk assessment, not automatic biopsy. Check TSH, characterize the nodule and cervical nodes by ultrasound, then use sonographic risk plus size and clinical context to decide FNA; suppressed TSH can redirect the workup toward functional imaging.
recognize: Rapid growth, firm/fixed nodule, suspicious nodes, hoarseness, prior neck radiation or strong familial thyroid-cancer syndrome raise concern.
Most incidental thyroid nodules are benign and over-investigation can cause harm.
differentiate: Abnormal thyroid function without a palpable structural abnormality is not a reason for routine ultrasound.
Nuclear medicine scanning is not the malignancy test for euthyroid nodules but can evaluate functional autonomy when TSH is suppressed.
assessment: Assess compressive symptoms, voice change, radiation/family history, thyroid symptoms, pregnancy and cervical nodes.
workup: Order TSH and thyroid/neck ultrasound; apply accepted ultrasound risk criteria and size thresholds for FNA and refer suspicious nodes appropriately.
management: Observe low-risk nodules at guideline-consistent intervals, biopsy those meeting criteria and refer suspicious/indeterminate cytology through endocrine/surgical pathways.
medicationSafety: Routine levothyroxine suppression for benign nodules is generally not justified because overtreatment harms can exceed benefit.
counselling: Explain why surveillance is active management and why not every nodule benefits from biopsy.
followUp: Track every recommended ultrasound/FNA/cytology result and adjust interval to the actual risk category.
examTrap: Biopsying every incidental nodule—or ordering ultrasound solely because TSH is abnormal with a normal thyroid examination.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid nodule biopsy is ultrasound-risk and size driven, not fear driven.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Endocrinology and Metabolism recommendations

title: Thyroid Cancer Follow-Up: Risk-Adapted Surveillance, Not Endless Scanning
bottomLine: Thyroid-cancer surveillance is risk adapted to histology, stage, treatment and response. Use the appropriate thyroglobulin/antibody and neck-imaging strategy after differentiated thyroid cancer and avoid routine broad imaging when biochemical/clinical risk is low; medullary/anaplastic cancers follow different markers and specialist pathways.
recognize: Rising thyroglobulin or new structural findings after differentiated thyroid cancer can indicate persistent/recurrent disease, but antibodies can interfere with thyroglobulin interpretation.
TSH targets are individualized to recurrence risk and treatment response rather than permanently suppressed in every survivor.
differentiate: Papillary/follicular differentiated cancer, medullary thyroid cancer and anaplastic disease have different surveillance markers/urgency.
Benign post-treatment neck changes should not automatically trigger repeated invasive testing without a risk-based interpretation.
assessment: Review pathology/stage, surgery/radioiodine history, recurrence risk, thyroglobulin/antibodies, TSH/levothyroxine plan, neck symptoms and prior imaging.
workup: Use neck ultrasound and biochemical testing at risk-appropriate intervals; cross-sectional/nuclear imaging is selected for biochemical or structural concern rather than routine use in every low-risk patient.
management: Coordinate endocrine/oncology/surgery follow-up; adjust TSH suppression to recurrence risk and harms such as AF/osteoporosis, and escalate rising biochemical/structural evidence appropriately.
medicationSafety: Excessive chronic TSH suppression can contribute to arrhythmia and bone loss; levothyroxine target must be intentional and reassessed over time.
counselling: Explain the surveillance plan and why fewer scans can be safer when recurrence risk and markers remain low.
followUp: Maintain closed-loop specialist surveillance with explicit ownership of thyroid hormone targets and pending imaging/biochemical results.
examTrap: Keeping every low-risk thyroid-cancer survivor maximally TSH-suppressed forever or ordering routine whole-body imaging without a clinical/biochemical reason.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid cancer follow-up becomes less intensive when risk and response justify it—but it never becomes ownerless.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada endocrine/nuclear medicine stewardship principles

title: Adrenal Insufficiency: Replace Cortisol, Recognize Crisis Early
bottomLine: Adrenal insufficiency may be primary or central and requires glucocorticoid replacement plus mineralocorticoid replacement only when aldosterone deficiency is present. Suspected adrenal crisis with hypotension, vomiting, severe weakness or altered consciousness is treated immediately with parenteral glucocorticoid and fluids—do not wait for confirmatory testing.
recognize: Fatigue, weight loss, postural symptoms, nausea, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia can occur; hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation support primary rather than central disease.
Chronic exogenous glucocorticoids can suppress the HPA axis and create secondary adrenal insufficiency.
differentiate: Primary disease impairs cortisol and often aldosterone; central disease usually preserves mineralocorticoid function.
Sepsis, GI illness and other shock states can mimic crisis, but treatment should not be delayed when adrenal crisis is plausible.
assessment: Assess steroid exposure/taper, autoimmune disease, pituitary symptoms, volume status, BP/orthostasis, vomiting, infection/surgery and pregnancy.
workup: When stable, use morning cortisol/ACTH and stimulation testing as appropriate plus renin/aldosterone for primary disease; in crisis obtain samples if feasible but treat first.
management: Use physiologic glucocorticoid replacement and fludrocortisone for confirmed primary mineralocorticoid deficiency; provide stress-dosing plans. Crisis requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone-equivalent therapy, isotonic fluids and precipitant treatment.
medicationSafety: Abrupt cessation after prolonged systemic steroids can precipitate crisis; fludrocortisone over-replacement can cause hypertension/edema/hypokalemia.
counselling: Provide emergency steroid card/medical identification, sick-day rules and injection training where applicable.
followUp: Review symptoms, BP/electrolytes, stress-dosing use and endocrine follow-up; reassess recovery of HPA axis after exogenous suppression when appropriate.
examTrap: Waiting for cortisol testing before treating a hypotensive vomiting patient with known adrenal insufficiency.
oneLinePearl: Adrenal crisis is a treat-first emergency; confirmation can follow resuscitation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism adrenal-insufficiency resources

title: Cushing Syndrome: Test When the Phenotype Is Discriminatory
bottomLine: Do not screen everyone with obesity, diabetes or hypertension for Cushing syndrome. First exclude exogenous glucocorticoid exposure, then test patients with multiple progressive or discriminatory features using validated hypercortisolism screening tests before trying to localize the source.
recognize: Wide violaceous striae, proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, facial plethora, unexplained osteoporosis, difficult hypertension/diabetes and growth deceleration in children are more discriminatory than obesity alone.
differentiate: Alcohol use, depression and severe obesity can produce pseudo-Cushing physiology; exogenous glucocorticoids are common and may be inhaled, injected, topical or hidden in supplements.
assessment: Review all steroid exposures, tempo of phenotype, menstrual/androgen symptoms, infection/thrombosis, fractures, psychiatric/metabolic complications and pregnancy.
workup: Use one of the validated first-line cortisol screening approaches appropriate to the patient and confirm abnormal results before ACTH-based/localizing evaluation.
management: Refer confirmed endogenous hypercortisolism to endocrinology; treat complications and underlying source. Taper exogenous glucocorticoids safely rather than abrupt cessation when suppression is likely.
medicationSafety: Abrupt chronic-steroid withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis; drug interactions and estrogen/pregnancy can affect some cortisol tests.
counselling: Explain why testing is targeted to a Cushing phenotype rather than used as a general obesity/hypertension screen.
followUp: Track metabolic, bone, infectious and cardiovascular complications during specialist evaluation/treatment.
examTrap: Ordering random cortisol or broad Cushing testing solely because a patient has obesity and hypertension without discriminatory features.
oneLinePearl: Cushing testing needs a Cushing phenotype—and the first question is always steroid exposure.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Endocrinology stewardship principles

title: Pheochromocytoma: Biochemical Proof Before Localization
bottomLine: Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma should be considered with episodic or sustained hypertension plus adrenergic spells, an adrenal mass or hereditary risk. Establish biochemical catecholamine excess with appropriate metanephrine testing before routine localization, and never start beta blockade before adequate alpha blockade in a confirmed catecholamine-secreting tumour.
recognize: Episodic headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, tremor/panic-like symptoms and labile hypertension are classic but not universally present.
Incidental adrenal mass, young onset or hereditary syndromic features can trigger evaluation even without the classic triad.
differentiate: Panic, hyperthyroidism, stimulant use, OSA and medication withdrawal can mimic adrenergic spells.
Nonfunctional adrenal incidentalomas are far more common than pheochromocytoma.
assessment: Review attack pattern, BP, medications/stimulants, family/genetic history, adrenal imaging history, orthostasis, pregnancy and cardiovascular complications.
workup: Use plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines under appropriate preanalytic conditions; interpret borderline results with medication/stress context and proceed to imaging after biochemical evidence or compelling specialist-directed circumstances.
management: Refer confirmed disease for endocrine/surgical management with preoperative alpha blockade, volume preparation and genetic evaluation as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Unopposed beta blockade can worsen vasoconstriction/hypertensive crisis; review drugs that interfere with catecholamine/metanephrine testing.
counselling: Explain why biochemical confirmation usually precedes repeated imaging and why medication preparation before surgery is essential.
followUp: Long-term biochemical/specialist surveillance depends on pathology/genetic risk because recurrence/metastatic disease can occur.
examTrap: Giving a beta blocker alone for severe tachycardia/hypertension in confirmed pheochromocytoma before alpha blockade.
oneLinePearl: Prove catecholamine excess, then localize—and alpha blockade comes before beta blockade.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism: Confirm Calcium-PTH Physiology, Then Assess Organ Impact
bottomLine: Primary hyperparathyroidism is persistent hypercalcemia with an inappropriately elevated or non-suppressed PTH after calcium status, kidney function, vitamin D and medication/familial mimics are considered. Management depends on symptoms, calcium severity, kidney/bone impact, age and surgical criteria—not PTH level alone.
recognize: Many patients are asymptomatic; nephrolithiasis, osteoporosis/fracture, renal impairment, constipation, weakness or neurocognitive symptoms can occur.
Lithium, thiazides and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia can complicate interpretation.
differentiate: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD/vitamin D deficiency occurs in a different calcium/renal context.
assessment: Assess stones, fractures/bone density, kidney function, calcium/vitamin D intake, family history, lithium/thiazides, pregnancy and symptoms of severe hypercalcemia.
workup: Confirm calcium appropriately and measure PTH, creatinine/eGFR, phosphate, vitamin D and urinary calcium when needed to distinguish FHH and assess surgical criteria; use imaging only for preoperative localization after biochemical diagnosis.
management: Refer patients meeting surgical indications for parathyroidectomy; monitor selected asymptomatic patients with structured calcium/renal/bone surveillance and manage hydration/medication contributors.
medicationSafety: Do not order parathyroid imaging to diagnose PHPT; thiazides/lithium can alter calcium physiology. Severe hypercalcemia requires acute treatment rather than waiting for elective workup.
counselling: Explain that PTH should normally suppress when calcium is high; a 'normal' PTH can therefore be inappropriate and diagnostic.
followUp: If monitored nonoperatively, track calcium, renal status and bone density at evidence-based intervals and revisit surgery if criteria develop.
examTrap: Ordering a sestamibi scan before biochemical confirmation—or dismissing a mid-normal PTH as normal physiology despite persistent hypercalcemia.
oneLinePearl: High calcium should suppress PTH; failure to suppress is the key physiologic clue.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada endocrine imaging stewardship principles
